While what I learned will definitely be of help to me in the future, I am still incredibly disappointed that I was essentially click baited into getting this course, especially when they even had a picture of a person using a VR headset in the thumbnail for this course.
The other major problem with this course is the amount of handwaving and lack of explanation of new topics the further into the course you get.
By the time you get to the 4th week, you'll be using things like Invoke() with no idea what it does or the meaning behind it, simply because you're following along the tutorial.

While at the beginning of the course there was plentiful explanations to be had on what new terminology was or how to use the different tools that were being discussed, a lot of the last two weeks of the course felt both rushed and underexplained, with a lot of glossing over of topics that felt important to understand just what was happening in the code.

While these two faults were pretty glaring, they did not prevent me from having a good time learning throughout this course, nor did they undercut any of the work that the team behind the course put into it.

I would definitely recommend this course if you already have a small amount of C# experience, through CodeAcadamy or the like, and if you want to get into learning how to code a game that IS NOT for VR purposes.

To what standard?
From which teachers?

She was sympathetic to broad tenets of Buddhism but I find no evidence she practised Buddhism.
The Golden Rule can be found in all faiths but beyond that I see no commonality.
The egalitarian claims of the TS are not substantially supported, either by empirical enquiry of its publications, or by the claims made by actual faiths.

I've been working on pronunciation for almost forty years and my primary fields of research were phonology and interphonology in language learning.
To help Brazilian EFL (English as a Foreign Language) students improve their pronunciation, I use phonetics and phonology as a tool.

While I acquired American English at the age of seven, I've always loved the sounds of the standard British accent, formerly known as RP (Received Pronunciation), especially when listening to BBC or UK voice actors.

Was your English accent affected by the Portuguese language at first?
If that's the case, Alison has produced an Udemy course to remedy your sound issues.

With Udemy courses I do not set my expectations too high, because you may never know, what can surprise you - positively or negatively.

It really is so different from instructor to instructor, how much overall information one gives and how much (s)he goes in the depths of different topics/instruments.

+ quick and short demonstrations of different instruments to see if you are maybe drawn to them

As a Japanese language learner, I find this course very helpful in providing contexts that are not always stated in textbooks.
I learned phrases suitable for business situations, and what to look out for to avoid being seen as rude.
The course is divided into easy-to-follow lessons with clear objectives.
It particularly provides useful phrases for remote-working situations, although anyone interested in improving their Business Japanese would still be able to gain valuable insights.
This was a very well thought and planned out course and I enjoyed it a lot.
Each of the 4 lessons all provided useful explanations, scenarios, and examples.
I really enjoyed analyzing native level conversations and working step by step to convert them to both "Polite" and "Very Polite" Japanese.

What I enjoyed most and thought was really interesting was how Mayo Sensei explained the subtle nuances and caution points that vocab, grammar, and even intonation have that you would not learn from a textbook.
The explanations really helped in knowing WHY things are said the way they are so that you can avoid coming off as rude or causing a misunderstanding with the person you are speaking to.

She also showed examples of what Japanese learners might usually say (or not say) that are grammatically correct, but are either not natural or not said at all and that may also convey impoliteness to the other person that the speaker did not intend.
It was those kinds of small but incredibly useful things that made Mayo Sensei's course really stand out to me.

When going through dialogue examples where we needed to convert certain parts to more formal forms, I thought it was great that Mayo Sensei provided hints first rather than going straight to the answer.
There were quite a few times where the hints helped me convert a section of dialogue correctly when I knew the conjugation needed, but not necessarily the best vocab to use.
It was also really helpful having the differences in conjugation/vocab explained for both "written" and "spoken" Japanese.
Another thing that I thought was really helpful were end of lesson reviews that helped me quickly and clearly see how to convert from casual to humble language.
While each Section was great, I personally enjoyed the lessons presented in Section 4 the most.

Some things that I think would be useful to the course would be: To maybe also show a table comparing the "written" vs "spoken" version of vocab during the end of lesson reviews, Have a quiz between parts 1 and 2 for both Section 1 and Section 2, and also increase the volume for Sections 1 through 3.
When going through the course, the volume of narration in Section 4 was much louder than in the first 3 which I actually appreciated because I was able to hear the lesson much better.
Other than the few points mentioned above, I didn't have any other issues with the course.
Overall, this was a wonderful and easy to digest Business Japanese course.
Mayo Sensei did a fantastic job providing practical dialogue scenarios and explaining the subtle nuances for various grammar/vocab that only a native Japanese speaker could understand and convey.
Mayo Sensei's enthusiasm and narration was infectious and motivating as well which made going through the course a lot of fun.

For many learners of Japanese, Keigo is a very intimidating aspect of the language, but thanks to this course, I feel so much more confident in my ability to correctly and politely communicate with all levels of people in a business or formal setting.
On top of that, I now also know how the choice of vocab, grammar, and intonation I use will also affect how the person I am speaking to thinks of me.

This is an advanced level course that I would absolutely recommend to anyone who wants to either use Japanese in a business setting, or just to be able communicate more politely in Japanese in general.
I will definitely be coming back to this course as a reference anytime I need to review or brush up on Keigo.
I look forward to more course from Mayo Sensei in the future!

I wanted conversation to keep me company while doing some canning and I got both -- great conversation and a bunch of canning accomplished.
So, one of the topics covered was about selecting a really good course name and why it matters.
And if I had to rename this course to fit my experience it would be:  "Sufi's Secret Sauce to Udemy/Online Teaching Engagement & Retention".
Why?
Well, it took a day for that thought to hit me.
You know, I wasn't even going to take this class when I first saw it.

I thought, "Mmmm, is this going to be another class that is an instruction manual that is spoken at me, just like any other class I've taken that is pushing the "how to succeed" or "this is the way I exceeded my expectations" story from someone who is sitting in front of a white background and then staring at me?"
But then I quickly remembered who is teaching the course.
So I looked at the course details and became intrigued.
This is the 5th course I have taken and completed from Sufani Garza and all of the others were not just learning, but fun and interesting.
And it seemed like my higher self was nudging me, like "you gotta do this one -- go ahead!"
So, I bought.
Then, iPhone, air pods and Google Home screen at the ready (sometimes I streamed it to Google Home to get a break from the air pods) and 50 lbs of tomatoes plus canning supplies at hand, I dove in.
I took it over 4 days and canned over 4 days (tomatoes, cherry pie filling and pulled pork -- a jar of pulled pork might be sandwiches for dinner tonight).

And here's the key takeaways:  Sufi is teaching you how to navigate Udemy, how to manage your expectations as an instructor, how make better choices, how to create quality videos, how to engage your audience, how to retain your audience, how to create your own "look and feel" and how to make everyone feel comfortable as they are watching and listening to you.
OK, so you might be thinking "What's so secret about that?"
Fair enough.
I'll tell you.
I could not figure out why I always feel so comfortable taking Sufi's classes.
I've mentioned this in other reviews -- it's like chatting with a good friend.

And -- full transparency -- I have purchased over 200 Udemy classes and completed many of them, but I consume some creators' courses fairly quickly after purchase while others don't get completed or wait for me to start them.
So, why is it that I have already purchased 12 classes from Sufi and completed 5 with a 6th in progress and a 7th I am going to start this evening?
I learned that answer by taking the course.

I learned what visually keeps me engaged.
I learned what it is about her style (although I already knew) that engages me from the beginning of her courses.
And I learned that she is real and genuine.
There isn't a "teacher Sufi" and a "person Sufi".
What you experience during her classes is who Sufani Garza is.
We live in a world where so much is smoke and mirrors or spruced up to appear as something it is not.
It is refreshing and interesting to experience a real person, teaching from experience, telling stories, encouraging success and reminding us that we can accomplish whatever we set out to do.
We just have to believe.
The sum up, I learned a lot of good  "whats", "hows", "whys", "what ifs" and all of the things I expected to learn.
But I also learned what the "je ne said quoi" is and how to create my own.

A general and brief idea about reading.
This course is essentially a pep talk for critical reading and its life-transforming positive value, but it doesn't do much to help one become such a reader if one isn't such a reader already.

The how-to aspects of critical reading are presented in this course as an endless parade of the usual bromides -- mark up the text, underline important passages, note definitions of terms, write notes in the margins, take note of important events and characters and their relationships with each other, note the steps of arguments, write summaries of chapters, write summaries of books, and on and on and on.
No help is offered to the student who may have questions about how to do these things (e.g., what makes a passage "important"?)
or is simply overwhelmed by the great number of different things supposedly required of the reader.
The instructor acknowledges that these recommendations might involve significant frustration and pain at first, but, he assures us, the journey gets easier over time.
Perhaps, but this course hasn't provided me with what I'd need in order to begin that journey.

St-Onge Lamoureux, 2012 SCC 57, [2012] 3

The Tarot deck consists of 78 cards with two major divisions, the Major Arcana and the Minor Arcana.
There are 22 cards in the Major Arcana and 56 cards in the Minor Arcana.
The Minor Arcana is composed of 4 suits; Pentacles, Swords, Cups, and Wands.
Each Minor Arcana suit contains 14 cards; 10 pip cards numbered ace to 10 and then 4 court cards.
The 4 suits correspond to the 4 elements; Earth, Air, Water, and Fire.
Pentacles deal with physical possessions, Swords deal with the mental realm, Cups deal with emotions, and Wands deal with the soul.
The court cards actually represent two elements, the element of the suit and the element of the court card.
Pages relate to earth, Knights relate to fire, Queens relate to water, and Kings relate to air.

For someone who was in and left a toxic relationship dynamic, identifying and being able to describe the "habits," "traits," "behavior dynamics," "red flags," and just overall feelings and experiences of being in this type of relationship is crucial.

This is the second part of a what was originally a very large single course on Learning Game Design that got broken into two pieces.
Some of the videos mention the original larger course, and there might be some confusion at times because of that.
Ideally you should take both of these courses in order, but you can skip around bit if you want to focus on particular topics, but you get the most out of it by doing it in order.
If you are totally new to the idea of doing game design, I would suggest starting with Dr. Pulsipher's more introductory course: Brief Introduction To Game Design.
There is occasional repetition across some of Dr. Pulsipher's eleven courses, but for the most part each course has plenty of new content.
Note that all of his courses have coupon codes on his own website (just Google pulsiphergames) ... and a couple of his courses are completely free this way!
Why should you take this course (these courses)?
Well, the main reason is that Dr. Pulsipher is an experienced game designer that has a wealth of real-world experience and knowledge to share.
Some of his game credits include Britannia, Valley of the Four Winds, Dragon Rage, and Sea Kings -- with a couple more hopefully coming out this year.
Dr. P is not an entertainer ... he is an educator.
So don't expect fanfare, rah-rah-rah, fancy animations, gimmicky presentations, or promises of how to get rich quick by designing games.
He will tell you about success stories in the industry like Reiner Knizia, but that you have a greater chance of winning the lottery than being the next Reiner Knizia.
Don't be put off by these cold hard facts ... Dr. Pulsipher tells you ... do game design because you love it, not because you have a pipe dream that you might get rich.
Do it because you love it!
(Dr. P actually has an entire course called the Joys of Game Design.)
So if you want to learn about the nuts and bolts of the actual process of game design, take these courses.
Ask questions within the course Q&A section ... he actually answers!
To supplement the courses you can read his book, watch his Game Design channel on YouTube, and take advantage of the wealth of knowledge & experience that he has to offer.
I have finished nine of his eleven courses so far, and I look forward to any additional courses he may publish in the future.

Product planning is often black magic.
A company has or is planning to have a product, or offer a service, that has either failed in the past or the company sort of shoots in the dark about what customers might accept and buy.
I have seen this several times.
It's really hard to turn the guesswork into a real process that helps to make the probability of acceptance significantly higher.
Finally, this course does just that.

It starts with an abundance of theory, maybe a bit too much, but as you get farther and farther through the course the theory becomes more concrete and finally in the last few sections you have a real path to how to plan.
Or in the specific case here, how to plan again, or pivot from your previous failed plans to a successful one where the company offers a successful product.
A lot of theory up front, granted, but concrete steps by the end.
This is a valuable course for any company offering a product or service, especially if they've seen less than full success in the past.

This course is essentially a series of webinars that were recorded live in front of a webinar audience and then broken up into individual lessons.

What I liked

It was very "look over the shoulder", hands-on stuff, so instead of just telling you things, Michel actually showed you how to do things, why and when you'd want to do them (or wouldn't want to do them), and showed some of the potential mistakes you might make.

The list of plug-ins and the run through of each of them was enlightening and, even though I thought I knew a lot, I discovered many gems both in the plug-ins and in interesting ways to use the plug-ins.
Michel goes through every recommended plug-in explaining what it's for, how to use it, why to use it and shows specific examples when appropriate.
I liked the way the webinar question and answer sessions were done and presented.

I liked the genial, informal, and friendly teaching style Michel uses and that, while he is clearly an expert in this topic, there was never a hint of the superior attitude that so many experts fall into and that impedes the transfer of knowledge and hinders learning.

What I didn't like

Since these were webinars that were split into lessons, I found several things I didn't like:

1.
Some of the lessons, particularly at the beginning were so short that it seemed that a lesson had barely started before it was time to do all the clicking necessary to start the next one.
A few of the lessons cut off in mid-sentence, while a few others had "dead air" at the end of them.

There was a lot of hands-on live demonstrations but many times the screen was so small it was hard to read and particularly hard getting the Web addresses (URLs) of many of the sites was difficult without a "stop, rewind and replay" a few times each -- a callout on the videos with the URL would be nice like was done at the beginning.
Also, a few times what Michel was showing was off the screen so you couldn't see them.
The list of plug-ins reviewed dragged on a little too long, cutting that down would have allowed more time for other things and more depth on some of the more complex things.
You'll notice that not many of the things I didn't like about the course had anything to do with the content of the course.
Michel well exceeded my expectations and the course was well worth the time I invested in it.
I certainly look forward to more courses from the Licorice Group and Michel Fortin.

For example, make certain your snow lines follow the contours of the mountains, and be prepared to lose your pencil lines several times.

Overall the course presents a good overview of Apache Storm, it definitely could be better though, I've left my feedback below:

Showing how to set up Storm within Docker would be a good section to add that feels missing.
The big data processing types and Lambda architecture are covered but it is done right at the beginning.
I would recommend a final module that talks about the scenarios in which to use Apache Storm and what the recommended criteria would be.
There is a section on When to Use Apache Storm and it provides some examples, but because these are early on and the examples aren't revisited with "what the spouts would be?"
and "what the bolt processing would do?"
at a high level they just feel like they were clip art slides thrown into the presentation.
Additionally in what circumstances would we use Trident vs Storm Spouts and Bolts?
is there any guidance to be offered?
Apache Storm also has a lot more ways to interact with it than just the Java methods shown.
There are some .Net Core ports of the Spouts, and Bolts.
As well as showing some examples for how to connect a message broker such as Kafka or RabbitMQ, they are mentioned but not touched on in any way.
These sections could even just be pointers for next steps for the viewer.

In the section explaining stream grouping:  The concepts are shown, it would also be a good idea to provide some real world examples, when working with just numbers it doesn't really portray enough to say what it could be used for.
For example could we do grouping based upon tuple priority or customer size?

Trident Joining Stream Tuples:  This section feels very rushed, and the input data is not well represented to the viewer, which leaves us in a state of "oh, those output numbers don't mean a lot to me, but sure you did something".
I would recommend re-recording this, slowing it down and re-explaining it both from the input and output data and process perspective.

Minor naggle for early lessons below and some tips to possibly  watch out for because Java has no unsigned integers like other languages, but it gets better as it goes on but teacher's English speaking is very clear and understandable and the pace is perfect for fundamental review and it definitely covers important, common interview topics, especially number manipulation and recursion.

(Here's the signed integer thing-->) In the first few lessons starting out (counting digits plus a few others), all the conditional statements to check if finished used a greater than zero check to tell whether the count was complete, but thanks to Java's inherent "simple" integer model, there is a logic hole: if the integer passed to the program is negative, the program will fail to count digits.
If the comparisons were all changed from less than zero to not equal to zero, the logic would pass and the digits of negative integers would count successfully.

Some of the other routines would also work with similar fixes, and students should not be surprised if an interviewer asks them how to fix the program for such a scenario, since negative or out-of-range integer inputs have been historically used to crash a number of Java-based websites as exploits.

I did learn a few things from this course, so it wasn't a waste of time, but I also felt like the things I learned were things I could have just googled and not paid for.

The reason I didn't google in the first place is because I was looking for more in-depth information on microphones in a nice clean way that went into the technical information without shoving me into the deep end of audio engineering where the learning curve is so high that I want to run screaming into the night.
Udemy is really great about flattening that learning curve.
And that's what I was eagerly looking forward to.
But this flattened the curve... a bit too much.
Yes, it's an overview.
And I should have seen that there was only 30 minutes of content.
But I'd still argue that this was like an overview of an overview.
The "basics" of audio engineering and microphones is still way more complex than this from what I quasi-learned in college.
Comparing it to running through a syllabus might be hyperbolic, but that's kind of how it felt to me.

If I had been designing this course, I would have gone into way more detail, showed examples, diagrams, done demos, illustrated what it sounds like when a mic is too close, too far away, in the sweet spot, etc, talked about clipping and noise reduction and pop-filters.
Even though I conceptually understand the polar patterns, what is the "font of the mic" and how do I know which way it's facing?
What are some examples of interfaces that provide phantom power?
Can you accidentally blow out a mic or damage a mic by plugging it into power you shouldn't--or can you really not do that because they don't give you the option?
I would have loved to see what these mics looked like, and where you place them based on the pattern and the instrument and style of microphone.
A lot of things were glossed over too--like "overheads."

I think I understand that that means overhead mics that capture the sound of the room, but I only know that because of my previous minimal recording experience--which others taking this course might not have.
For the total novice, they wouldn't have known what that meant.

The person who gets the most out of this course as it is--its target audience--would most likely be people who have -zero- background knowledge of mics and audio engineering, and with that in mind, glossing over these terms would have been confusing and not actually that educational.
For Section 3, the one section I really had zero knowledge in, I really wanted visuals or a demo or something, because otherwise, I have no idea what these terms really mean in action.

So in conclusion--and based on the description of the course and not my own personal expectations--this course was pretty good, but confusingly targeted for a person who simultaneously has no knowledge of mics but also somehow has a working understanding of terms that are mentioned but not explained.

The instructor is not a native English speaker which, in itself, is not a huge problem, but what is a huge problem is the incredibly poor standard of the recording of this material.
There are so many occasions where the instructor makes mistakes with this words and then repeats his paragraph again.
Ordinarily, you would expect that the instructor would edit the video content in such a way that these mistakes are removed, where-as here, we get a repetition of nonsense.
There are many occasions where the instructor seems quite concerned about the runtime of his video recording and keeps checking the duration.

There are many occasions where the instructor says "I will see you in the next video" only to then, either intentionally, or by accident, carries on recording whilst he tries to figure out what is going wrong with the image he has been working on.

Section two of this course is utter gibberish, having just installed Photoshop and had an incredibly fast run through of some of the tools, the instructor goes completely off topic for an entire section.

During this section, you are bombarded with flickering images which have been, presumably, taken from Haiku.com or Google images which may relate, slightly, to the over-arching course title but have no bearing at all on what the instructor is currently talking about.
In the following sections, you are introduced to the concept of copying images from Flappy Bird.
I am still at a loss as to why you would painstakingly try to replicate, exactly, these images - if you wanted a copy, simple "copy" and "paste" it.
The audio in section 5 is attrocious, if you can imagine someone talking into a muffled baked bean tin, that is the closest analogy to the experience I could give.

The final lecture, lecture 25, has the familiar "See you in the next lecture" message at the end, when the following lecture loads, it congratulates you for completing the course on "mobile game design"?
All the way through this course there are many generalizations and assumptions and no clear instruction at all, which leads you to really question this instructors knowledge and experience.
On a related note, whilst he introduces himself and Benjo Sabban, if you check the username for his course on Udemy it comes up under the name of /rafaeldebelen, seems odd.

A Google search of this instructor leads us to find that he has created about a dozen courses of all which have incredibly low ratings on Udemy, these are then linked to and re-appear on numerous other online training websites.

If there was an option to rate this course with a zero I would still choose the half a star option, as someone who had never used Photoshop before (although I have used other similar packages) there were a couple of snippets of information which I could take away and use, but these are very heavily outweighed by the poor flow, information, and instruction of this course.
I would not recommend this course to anyone unless you are considering creating your own course on Udemy, and want to see how "not" to do it.

At best this course should be "free" on the Udemy marketplace, or more ideally, this and Benjo / Rafael's other courses should be reviewed by the Q&A/Standards Team at Udemy and removal of them all should be considered.
On a final note, an announcement was made 3 years ago which mentions the addition of two Flappy Bird images to the downloadable resources.
These images do not appear to be available under a Creative Commons license and are therefore, presumably, subject to copyright laws.

No doubt like many of the other students of this course, I signed up in order to find out a little bit more information about Swift.

The course was sold as an introduction to the language, so I wasn't expecting an in-depth tutorial that would on its own enable me to become a Swift developer, rather some examples of the new syntax with some examples of how to use this new language to build some (very simple) programs.
Unfortunately however, the course didn't even meet this expectation.
I should point out that, certainly in the email where I saw this course advertised, it was sold as being suitable for programmers of all levels.
I have some experience with a few languages, including some low-level Objective-C, but I found that the pace that the instructor raced through certain concepts left me feeling a little lost at times.

This course aims to showcase every single element of the Swift language (which should be great), but it does so utilising only Xcode's new Playground feature and as a result of this, no meaningful programming happens at all.

At one stage in the course, the instructor says something the implies that he doesn't expect you to have done any iOS programming before, yet in the penultimate chapter (where he finally works on a simple app), he assumes an almost intimate knowledge of Xcode and prior Objective-C experience.
This course is also already out of date.
In one of the very first lectures the instructor even tells you how to download the Xcode 6 beta, despite the fact that it is now on public release.
As such, elements of the IDE do not look on the videos how they have ended up in the final release.
There is even one lecture where the functions that the instructor uses didn't even make it into the final version of the language.
Luckily Xcode provides prompts to allow you to use the correct code, but to release this in a course that people are paying for is sloppy.
The reason why this course has earned a 3 star review from me and not 2 is that I was able to follow most of it without any trouble.
So whilst I feel that this course is actually no use for a beginner, it does at least do the job for intermediate programmers and up.
However, I don't really feel like I have learned much from this course.
The lack of contextualised and fully fleshed out examples means that none of the code used has really stuck with me (apart from the basic syntax).
In general, this is not a particularly good course.
If you are interested in finding out a little about Swift, by all means have a look.
But please do not waste your money on this course if you intend to use it to learn, I'm sure there are far better courses out there designed for that purpose.

‚Äúvar x = new Array(5);‚Äù for example doesn't put the number 5 into an array, it creates an array with 5 elements, all undefined.

I'm currently evaluating on switching to Photon on my project's networking, because UNET is not working perfect yet (latency issues mainly).
I saw this course on sale and decided to sign up.
It did save me some time to set Photon up for a quick project (vs reading Photon's manual and applying it to my project).
If a quick intro to Photon is what you're looking for, I can certainly recommend this course.
It doesn't go very deep, but if you are already familiar with Unity and UNET, you shouldn't have any issues to get it up and running, and from there you can probably continue on your own.
Now, the course advertises that it can be "easily understood by absolute beginners".
I don't think this is entirely accurate.

Students can of course write along and get the same results as in the videos, but I don't think all concepts are properly introduced and explained in proper depth, and someone new to Unity or coding might have to depend on google a lot to clear some topics.
There are other courses here in Udemy that can give you a much nicer/smoother introduction to Unity.
I think there was another student that complained about the instructor's accent.
I'm not an English native speaker but had no trouble understanding at all.
But you can always check this on the intro videos before buying.

Additionally, a few things I believe the course could use improvement on (and why I believe absolute beginners should start with something else):

- Coding is not very neat and tidy.

Could be simple stuff like organizing public / private variables in an orderly manner or variable/method capitalization, or things like using values within code that could be public to be able to edit them in the inspector or adding the whole Menu inside the Networking script.
Nothing extremely serious for the scope of this course, but if you're very organized when write code you might not like this.
And if you plan on continuing this project into a bigger one, later on it will get messy to fix or modify things.
Considering how powerful Unity UI can be, and how messy GUI can get, it would be better and easier if this course's Menu system was done with Unity UI.
- The whole point of Unity's prefabs is for you to hit the "Apply" button when you make changes.
This course disregards that, and deletes/replaces prefabs all the time.
Again not a big deal, but if you're aiming at beginners you should point them to right working practices.
- I think it could be nice if a powerup shot is added, or an enemy special shot, that allows to fire projectiles in 30¬∞ angles or something.
To properly show students how it's done and how it's applied on a network.
Or adding lives, and ending the game for players if lives <= 0.

- The final game you get ends up with some rather serious bugs (players colliding to each other at spawn if no one moving, player bullets disappearing when hitting other players, and I believe the coin sound won't trigger to all clients, etc.)
which a beginner will struggle to fix.
The game doesn't need to be complete, but 1) it should fix serious issues, 2) should be closer to the one published on the App Store.

Despite the comments (which are mainly to help the instructor polish the course), I still recommend the course for anyone looking to get a quick overview on how a multiplayer shooter works with Photon, or as an additional course for a Unity shooter game.

"Nice Guy Syndrome Recover" - Course review

Disclaimer: I was given access to this course to leave an honest and fair review.
No incentives for a positive review were given.
What I have posted here is my honest review of this course.
First of all, no matter how good a course is, it's meaningless if you don't act upon it.
You can consume the material and be impressed with the content, but if you make no changes to yourself as a result of your learning, nothing happens.
So, TL: DR review of this course?
It's good, very good.
It's well presented, well constructed and far more relevant and practical than I first thought.
Now the detailed review.
I'm a teacher by trade, and I know how important it is to get any learning material prepared, delivered and into the hands of someone who can use it.
I look at all the courses I buy and self-improvement books through that lens.
I've spent lots of money on courses that promise a lot yet still don't deliver.
Conclusion: there are critical areas in which this course excels, making it very important in my personal development.
1 - Relevant.
The best course in the world isn't going to be helpful to you if it's not directly relevant.
One real eye-opener was that this course was relevant but was even more relevant than I expected.
The first part of the learning really drove home how embedded some of my behaviours and thoughts were.
Although I know this course 'should' be useful, I didn't realise how much I 'needed' it.
2 - Grounded in common sense and relatable scenarios.
I've bought a few of Mr Munro's books and courses before.
I've also listened to a lot of his podcast material.
What I respect most about his work is that it's no-nonsense, no BS.
It's entirely without fanfare and 'sizzle' - this course is all 'steak'.
There's no fluff and no timewasting sales pitch for anything else produced by the author.

Here are my main gripes:

* I am not sure at what level this course is aimed at
A beginner would struggle to follow the course if they were completely new to SQL.
If you were already familiar with SQL and want to see how TSQL differs, the pacing is slow and the differences are barely covered.

* Very slow delivery
The speed of these videos has been slowed down.
The chap giving them sounds like he is having a stroke and I had to increase speed to 2x to make it bearable.
A few videos are padded with 10+ seconds of empty time at the end.
Every video begins with the instructor selecting the correct database.
This takes up a good minute of time and is completely unnecessary after the first couple of videos.
The MAX and MIN videos are for some reason separate despite sharing 95% of the same content.
I am convince that the producer of this series has tried to inflate the course time to make it seem more comprehensive than it actually is.

* Poor explanations given:
What the GO keyword does was very unclear, which is a shame given that it is specific to TSQL

The video on sorting by multiple columns was explained very badly.
No examples are given to show that the table is sorted by the first column and then if these values are the same, it is subsequently ordered by the second column.
Section on joins was very lacking in information.
Full outer join is mentioned in the conclusion of this section despite not being covered anywhere.
There was no explanation on what a stored procedure is.
The instructor refers to the example database having multiple schema's but never covers what a schema is.
He also uses a view but gives no explanation about what a view is.
* Some of the examples used to highlight queries were poorly chosen.

The left outer join query did not show what happens when the right table does have a corresponding row.The right outer join query did not show what happens when the left table does not have a corresponding row.

* Sloppy mistakes
In many places, mistakes are made that should have been edited out.
The summary for the filtering section is actually the summary for the sorting section.
The summary for the aggregate function section is actually a repeat of the SUM explanation video.
On the insert section, the instructor confuses the primary key column with the column numbering provided in SQL Server Management Studio.
Frequent spelling mistakes (holyday rather than holiday was my favorite).
I would recommend one of the many other SQL courses on Udacity over this one.
Whilst they may not be for TSQL, the differences between the two dialects are negligible.

I found this course from Chris to be interesting, entertaining and useful.

One of the reasons is that he spends time explaining concepts which I had taken for granted ‚Äì such as the physical process of ageing, its link to frailty and tips and techniques to combat the unwanted effects of getting older.

The video clips from other experts add to this base of information, as do the interviews with Chris (yes, another Chris) who had made a massive change to his own life by increasing his fitness, and reducing his fatness, from being obese at age 50.

To be fair there are others who have also lost a substantial amount of weight over a period of time (Adele for example) but Chris Z is the only one as far as I know who has lost weight AND replaced a lot of the fat with muscle.
Hence the ‚Äòfat to fit‚Äô rather than ‚Äòfat to less fat‚Äô!
The pictures, news articles and video clips (not least the picture of the trophy cabinet!)
show Chris‚Äôs success in the transformation.

Add to that the fact that this was all done at middle-age (when weight is a lot harder to lose and poor eating routines are well embedded in the sedentary lifestyle) then that is a remarkable achievement.
The cutaways to countryside shots add to the calming effect, and provide time for the viewer to reflect on what has been explained and demonstrated.
The opportunity to ask questions via the Q&A function is also useful, and provides a direct link into Chris (the first Chris!)
to tap his extensive knowledge base.
The varied locations used, and the selection of other videos, ensure that none of the lectures become a monotonous time of him lecturing the viewer by constantly speaking to camera.
There is always something coming up that is a little different.
The entertainment aspect is helped by Chris‚Äô rather dry sense of humour.
It takes a little getting used to, but you can see how he brings a light touch occasionally to lift what I think can be a dry and heavy subject.
Finally, the closing segments showing Chris performing different exercises and activities over a multiple-day period is useful on a practical level.
There certainly is a substantial element of instruction here, combined with a feeling that he wants the viewer to know that if he can do it, then you can do as well.

The course is advertised as ‚ÄòFrail to fit in 50 lectures‚Äô but I get the feeling that new lectures are being added as the course progresses ‚Äì not least the ‚Äô30 day section‚Äô which only covers the first few days.
This means that the course will be updated on an ongoing basis which will make the information even more current.
In summary, I would recommend this course to anyone that is concerned about the ageing process, especially the negative aspects, in themselves or in others.
It will add to your knowledge in an interesting and entertaining way, and will help you to make those first steps in fighting frailty for yourself.

> Why does C++ separate .h and .cpp for the same class?
After some research it turns out these are related to the C++ compiler behavior and the philosophy of it, e.g.
C++ splits code into two parts: the ".h" file declares things and is used/included as a class signature/interface for other classes; the ".cpp" file defines those things e.g.
class functions, operator overloads, etc.
When you change a function in ".cpp" but keep the same signature in ".h", then other files which call this function or include the ".h", they don't need to be recompiled.
Its purpose is separate compilation and easier parallel compilation.

The most disappointed I am with the player animator.
First of all we are missing some states.
In the game it is possible to aim or shoot while running, but since we do not have states/animations for them, it looks very stupid, if you try to do that in game.
So, we would need to either add those missing states/animations or prevent the player from aiming and shooting while running in the code.
We are also missing some transitions.
If we for example start running right after shooting or reloading, the player will just slide forward for many seconds before finally starting to run.
Secondly, the player animator is not working at all.
When the player is shooting, the animator should ALWAYS be in "Shoot" or "ShootWalk" state, but in reality we can be also in "(aiming)Idle" or "(aiming)Walk" state when shooting.
The ONLY reason it LOOKS like working is that we are using aiming animation also for shooting.
If we used separate shooting animations in Shoot and ShootWalk states, it would be very obvious how badly this animator is working.
The instructor noticed this problem in the video, but instead of fixing it, he just added new transitions from "(aiming)Idle" and "(aiming)Walk" states to "(aiming) Recharge" state and back.
After that "fix" we now have FOUR transitions starting from "(aiming) Recharge" state and they all have only one (same) condition: Reloading=false.
So, let us assume, that the animator is in the "(aiming) Recharge" state and then in the code we set Reloading to false.
Which one of these four transitions Unity will select now?
Yes, it could be any of these four, so we definitely need to add more conditions to these transitions.
Also we do not need so many parameters in the player animator as we have now.
I would replace "IdleAim", "AimWalk" and "ShootWalk" parameters with just "Aim", which would simplify C# code.
Then for example instead of condition AimWalk=true we would have conditions Walk=true & Aim=true & Shoot=false etc.
Lastly a word about C# code in this course.
The instructor is using camelCase notation everywhere in the C# code when naming functions and variables, which is a good thing.
However, when the instructor is naming class functions, he is most of time starting them with capital letter, but randomly - without any logic - starts some of them with small letter.
Same thing with class variables.
If we decide to start function names with capital letter (like people usually do in C#), then we should do that everywhere in the code.
And if we decide to start class variable names with small letter, then we should not randomly start some of them with capital letter.
Otherwise the code will look VERY unprofessional.

Independent thinkers who do not rely on partisan rhetoric, from either party, are left to question the criteria upon which they base their beliefs.

That's why Bob Galante's "History Doctor" series is important: it provides significant information and historical precedent upon which to base judgments about what's going on these days, stripped of partisan affiliation.
It gives perspective.
In his series of chapters on the Bill of Rights, for example, Bob presents the background for the fundamental additions to our Constitution which have so greatly changed our lives.

With clearly presented historical facts and a carefully measured distance from making judgments, he delineates the context of each new Bill as they presented themselves, first for consideration and ultimately for adoption, to be incorporated into the framework of our legal system and forming a substantial part of its presence today.

Who will benefit from this course:

- People who want to speed up their workflow and avoid creating repeated or tedious details every time they start a sculpt

- Anyone who really wanted to make a special brush for times when the basic brushes aren't quite what they need

- Those who want to make tiling textures in Zbrush and to use them or finalize them in other software

Who may not benefit from this course:

- Absolute beginners, this course does not teach you the basics of the UI or sculpting it is strictly for learning these tools which will be a big help once you learn the basics

- Veterans of the software may already know this stuff, however it may teach you an alternate method of doing these things a bit faster

When I saw this course being available, it was almost an instant buy for me as I have been interested in using octrees for navigation for quite some time now.
What I expected was that as a final result we'd be able to have an efficient octree solution for navigation.

While it is true that the in the final result it is possible to choose a destination inside an octree and see the AI fly to, it has several issues:
1) the AI often flies through cubes/planets, which should be impassable.

So there is no local collision avoidance ( I realize that this is not a topic of this course but it seems like local collision avoidance should go hand in hand with calculating the path through the octree).
2) the path taken in most cases seems illogical.
You can visually see a straight path to the destination but the AI flies through nodes sometimes on the other half of the space making zig zags everywhere.
I think the second issue is caused by how neighbours of a node are found.
The method was very quick to implement and easy to understand but it fails to find all of the neighbours.
This results in illogcial paths for the AI.
I expected to see an implementation that is complex but actually works (this was even mentioned in the video).
Not necessarily related to octrees, but the code written is also of low quality: the C# standards are not followed and in many places it is very unoptimized (eg.
2 GetComponent calls of the same component on 2 consecutive lines).
And the architecture of the code written could be much better as well.
The course gave me some idea on how an octree could be set up and the space split up with crude navigation, I expected a much more thorough course about octrees.
Something that would prepare me for the "real world".
I would not use the final state of the project of this course in my live projects and there would still be a lot to be done before this was the case.
I hope the course gets updated in the future and will go more in-depth.

Zack Van Niekerk, like most of us, has a lifetime‚Äôs experience of learning.
Unlike many who move into teaching, though, he has embraced this experience.

Rather than distracting himself with how language is taught in schools, how it was taught to him and what could be improved, Zack approaches the problem of language-learning from first principles, asking how we learn when we‚Äôre not even consciously doing so.
This leads to some pretty amazing results.
Most language-learning resources online focus on the basic building blocks of the language ‚Äì vocabulary, grammar, and so on.
This course breaks that mould, instead offering learners means to teach themselves throughout their everyday life.
Much has been made in debates over language-learning on the importance of immersion, and while Zack avoids the word, he instructs us to engage actively with our target language throughout our day.
How should we do this?
The answer is, as with much on this course, surprisingly simple: we learn the way a baby learns.
This is perhaps the most enlightening aspect of Zack‚Äôs Spanish course.
What so many casual language learners miss is the importance of forming a ‚Äòneed‚Äô for their target language.
Babies, Zack points out in one of his easy-to-follow, engaging videos, learn through necessity.
They need to communicate something.
His innovation is to suggest that we do the same.

Whether by taking the effort to immerse ourselves in a community of target language speakers, or by something as simple as identifying objects in our daily life we‚Äôd like to be able to translate, we can actively create this need for ourselves.
Helpfully, all this means we can take learning not only outside the classroom, but outside the confines of teaching at all.
It‚Äôs exciting stuff, and there‚Äôs a lot more on offer here than just this, including some examples of especially useful vocabulary to help guide you towards creating needs for new words.
Overall, though, this course is a fascinating and novel way to think about learning a language, inviting us to explore and giving us practical tips on how to do so rather than rote instruction.

Yes, I've used Max for years but it always is nice to see someone else work and pick up different tips and workflows along the way.

The course has some good tips that I didn't know about but also some odd techniques that overcomplicate things and severe omissions of some features that make some of this easier than how it's presented here.

The stuff about the UVW Map modifier alone was worth the cost of entry because I hadn't used it before (instead doing everything in the Unwrap UVW modifier) but the UVW map does do a better job at getting you properly proportioned planar maps vs the Unwrap UVW modifier's version so that was a nice find.
Other aspects of the course were odd.

My biggest issue with the course is that while he does show you how to enable the checkerboard texture and also the checkerboard with letters, he spends most of the course without a texture applied to the model and frequently just disables it after he's done tweaking a certain bit.
I find that having an Unwrapping Grid Texture always applied while doing your unwrap is hugely important for getting a quick idea of how the proportions are and which direction the UV's are facing.

Doing it without a texture applied at all makes it hard for a newcomer to actually understand how the UV's affect the way a texture is applied to a model and it really feels like you're flying blind without having it enabled through the whole process.
I found his section about Cylindrical unwraps was massively overcomplicated as well.

He has you do the cylinder unwrap with the UVW Map modifier's cylinder unwrap which by default causes some polygons to stick out of the edges and that he then spends a lot of time breaking them off and stitching back into their proper place, when the Unwrap UVW version of the cylinder projection lets you easily rotate the projection gizmo to avoid those stick-out bits AND gives a live update of what the UV's looked like and where the edges were.

During the section about dealing with overlapping UVS he also does this whole thing with the relax tool (which didn't work for me in the way it did on his video so perhaps something changed) but really could have done it a lot more cleanly by simply loop selecting the edges for the part of the UV's that were overlapping and bringing them straight up or down, rather than moving a bunch of stuff around and having to manually re-align it which would have a less precise result.

In general it feels like he neglected some of the more modern tools that the Unwrap UVW modifier provides to make things more precise even though some of the UVW Map options he showed were pretty useful.

The section about seam tools and Quick peel DID increase my understanding of those tool which was great, and that in and of itself was good, but the model he uses to demonstrate them on, the pipe, could easily be much more accurately unwrapped in basically one click using the "unfold strip from loop" tool inside of Unwrap UVW and I do wish he had at least mentioned that as an option.
It doesn't work for every scenario but it is an important topic to know.
The lack of any usage of "Flatten by Polygon Angle" during the architecture option also felt like a big omission since that's the bread-and-butter of a quick but basic unwrap.

In general he opts for buttons hidden in menus and right-clicks and while some of those do open up more precise functionality he ignores a lot of UI icons on the UV editor that do the same thing but more conveniently and while it is good to know the underlying functions, those UI icons are front and center because they're the types of things you'd probably want to use more frequently.
The character section is pretty good and probably the best bit section.

He does a good job of showing the different ways to make seams and how the placement of seams affects how the UV"s are generated when you use the Quick Peel tool and I was really impressed with how cleanly the UV's generate as long as you have good seams.

I was however, hoping we would explain the Pelt tool and also how to use the blue pins that the peel tool generates to adjust things since those have been things I've historically struggled with, and having those options neglected was frustrating since character unwrapping is one of the more complex topics and this was otherwise the cleanest section in the course.

The provided FBX models also seemed to have some normal weighting issues which isn't a huge deal since it's just an unwrap course, but it does make certain parts of the models overly dark and I had to slap an edit normals modifier on the models and hit reset for the lighting to work properly, which is somewhat of an advanced technique a newcomer might not know about.

Overall I did learn a couple decent tricks and that's always worth it but I think a newcomer trying to learn more about UV's would be a bit confused by some of what he does and would probably walk away with some less-than-optimal practices.

This might be decent if you already know what you're doing to an extent but want to take it a little further and pick up some new tricks but I do think it neglects some good tools and I was hoping it would be a bit more comprehensive on some things I've been curious about.
There are a number of buttons, tools and icons that just aren't covered that I would have liked to know the functions of.

For example, I've only ever used the "Stitch:Custom" tool for my stitching because the other stitch buttons seem to break things, so finding out what those other ones were meant to do would have been helpful.

There are also a number of interesting-sounding options in the UVW Map modifier that go unexplained, but at least seeing that they're there gives me a springboard to go looking for deeper information.

This course begins with a good grounding in Go, the basics are covered well, and despite an occasionally rushed narrative the basics are easy to follow and understand.
Unfortunately, as things progress more complex concepts are introduced and its here where the divergence in understanding truly occurs.
It appears almost an exponential relationship between the complexity of the subject matter and the simplicity and comprehensiveness of the lesson delivery.
In short, the instructor becomes more and more hurried to deliver the lessons the more complex they become.
By the end there is far to much omitted and unexplained that the course just falls into a matter of sit back and watch something happen rather than take it all in.
Larger swathes of code are pasted from previous lessons and whole new sections are pasted in with the minimal of explanation, then the code is run and the next lesson repeats the process.
During the sections that benefit from individual analysis, this is not such an issue since each subject may be viewed independently.

However the real issue arises with the so called "Building an App" section (7 & 8)

Here for each additional lesson, instead of the usual comprehensive way of building an app from the ground up, and adding to the code base, the teacher chooses to write a brand new version of the app for each lesson , first by copying and pasting from the previous lessons then by pasting large new lines of code into it with only the slightest of information.
This is not so much building an app, as watching an app being edited again and again, but with no full understanding on what is going on.
This is my main criticism, and it feels as though the app section was simply thrown in to the course to make up time.
It would have been far better to simply focus on explaining the more complex Golang features in greater depth, and leave building an App to a later course.
The App section did little to help understand many go features, especially not those covered in the earlier sections of the course.
There is no doubt that the Instructor is skilled.
At times his accent made things a little difficult to understand, especially at the speed of the narrative, but he was generally clear and concise.
There is courteous and prompt replies to questions, usually in a day or so, and the approach to students is good.
It was just disappointing that the course failed to really deliver on its title.
I would not recommend this course as an example of Building an App in Go, and not necessarily as a generally comprehensive course on Go, this would be better marketed as a quick overview of Go.
However, with this instructor, if they dropped the app section and focused on more fundamentals, more in depth explanation and less prewritten examples,  I would certainly recommend the course.

I've tried many highly-rated guitar courses on Udemy, and this one really gives me the impetus to keep going.

WHAT PROBLEMS IF FACED WITH LEARNING TO PLAY GUITAR:
(1) I thought I was hopeless with any musical instrument (except with a little recorder), I tried playing with an acoustic and it hurt so much I gave up
(2) I am a very petite Asian female with small hands, I'm playing an electric (Traveler's Guitar) due to its light weight, ease on fingers, and having a full-scale fretboard (meaning I can transition more easily to other guitars if I would like to in the future)

WHY I LOVED THIS COURSE:
(1) When courses start right off the bat with chords, I find that my fingers need much more dexterity to change between and I have not yet the muscle memory to instinctively get my fingers on the right strings for even simple chords, it's taken me over a month and I'm still struggling to transition from E Major Chord to A Major Chord (and back) seamlessly.
I wish there were lessons to help me build my finger strength first.

This one allows me to fret basic notes easily with one finger and slowly building to power chords with 2 fingers
(2) I'd feel much more motivated being able to play a practice piece that sounds like a song; it may not be well-known pop songs but at least something that makes me sound like I'm playing rather than repeating one or two notes or chords for stretches of time.
This course gives you just that; a practice piece for every lesson with backing tracks to boot!
(3) I would at least want to be able to read tabs and learn a little bit of music theory along the way, eventually being able to read musical notation.
All the notes accompanying every lesson provides all the notation and tabs.

WHAT TO BEAR IN MIND WHEN TAKING THIS COUSE:
(1) This course is for total beginners who want to get started playing, but find it overwhelming sifting through all the guitar courses available, this is really a solid place to start, the instruction couldn't be clearer and Paul's pacing is just spot on!

(2) This course gives you everything you need to start playing and learning a little bit of theory, tabs, fingering techniques, and picking
(3) It covers power chords (5 chords) only, you need to look elsewhere if you are trying to learn many other chords
(4) The music you produce sounds good (or similar to demo) only with overdrive or distortion effects (thankfully my guitar has those effects built in) so those with a basic electric guitar might want to get an amp with those effects or a pedal.

(5) Those with small hands (like kids or ladies) might find the taught finger positioning unwieldy and really difficult to play without major buzzing or silenced notes, I would change a bit of the finger positioning for consistency (like always use middle finger on 2nd fret, ring finger on 3rd fret, power chords that span across 3 frets I will involve my pinky but you need to build strength on it first)
(6) I practice all the lessons I've previously learned to ensure I can read the notes and also the tabs before moving to next lesson where something is new.
I do not proceed unless I could really play the practice piece well with the right tempo alongside the backing track.
THANK YOU Paul, hope you have more video lessons in the future as I would love to continue learning from you!

I have just completed this course, and found it both helpful and illuminating.

The course takes a new and innovative approach to exploring positive mental health by organising the curriculum around five core components - challenge, creativity, character, composure and connection (the 5 C's).

Each of these is then examined in some depth and detail, and is accompanied by case studies, detailed notes, links to further reading and a range of tasks and activities contained in a module companion E-book.

I found that the module companion E-book was an excellent way of jotting down my own ideas and thoughts as the lessons unfolded, as well as being a useful tool to keep track of my own learning and development around the 5 C's.

I really enjoyed being able to 'dip in' and out of the course material and go at my own pace, and found the prompt questions and reflective activities were enormously helpful in identifying what the topics meant to me on a personal level as well as flagging up the areas I needed to do more reading and work on.

Theories, methods and the evidence base to support application in practice were clearly explained, and there were some excellent signposts to the sources drawn on, making it easy for participants to do their own further reading and research outside of the course.

What I found particularly interesting were the concepts and approaches that were new to me that I hadn't come across before (for example, 'Acceptance Commitment Theory') as well as the way the presenters summarised the more 'tried and tested' theories and methods I was familiar with.
These were all explained in a clear and accessible way, and when combined with the structured questions in the E-book were a good way to apply the learning from the on-line lectures.

The simple but very effective exercise at the end of each section  where you rate yourself on a scale of 1-10 under all 5 of the core components, and then bringing it all together at the end in your 'personal star' was a very powerful way to see at a glance which of the 5 C's you might need to reflect on and pay some attention to.

Overall, a thoughtful and thought-provoking course about positive mental health that has encouraged me to think about this subject more deeply and given me some practical tools and tips that will help me professionally and personally.

This means that some of the utility functions in lodash have lost some of their appeal due to some new syntactic sugar provided by ES6/ES2015 that was inspired by libraries like lodash and that are now available natively in JavaScript (which can improve performance once the browsers and other runtime environments like Node.js fully support ES6/ES2015).
Nevertheless, there is way more to lodash that is not integrated in even the latest JavaScript spec so the library will continue to evolve and remain very useful.
This course is a very quick way to evaluate the potential of using lodash in your coding workflow.
